content:
I’m really sorry about your wife. What you’ve done with your tools, your father’s watch, and the cat arrangements sounds like a very kind way of looking after the people around you.

I’ll treat this as “if I die, or if I become unable to manage things.” If any of this is because you’re feeling hopeless, alone, or thinking about ending your life, please treat that as urgent and speak to someone today:

- If you’re in immediate danger, call your local emergency number or go to hospital/A&E/ER.
- UK: Samaritans 116 123, NHS 111, 999 if urgent  
- US/Canada: call or text 988  
- Australia: Lifeline 13 11 14  
- Elsewhere: tell me your country and I can help you find local support.

If you’re safe, here is a practical checklist for making your affairs clear. Rules vary by place, so for the legal documents themselves—especially the will and power of attorney—it’s worth speaking to a local lawyer/solicitor, notary, or estate-planning professional. But this will give you a clear path.

## 1. Name the key people

Make a short list of who you want to deal with each area. It helps to have a backup for each role.

- **Executor of your will**: the person who deals with your estate after you die.
- **Backup executor**: in case the first person can’t or won’t.
- **Property/finance attorney**: the person allowed to manage money and property if you become unable to do so.
- **Backup attorney**.
- **Health/medical decision-maker**: the person who can make medical decisions if you cannot.
- **Cat carer**: who feeds and cares for your cat if you are away or unwell.
- **Backup cat carer**.
- **GP/doctor**: so they know who to contact.
- **Trusted neighbour/friend**: who has keys and can check on you or the cat.
- **Funeral contact**: who you want to call first about your funeral arrangements.

If you don’t have family nearby, neighbours can be useful, but it’s often best to choose people who are stable, reliable, and willing. If you’re thinking of using a neighbour as executor, ask them first and make sure they understand it can be a serious responsibility.

---

## 2. Make or update your will

A will is the main document for saying who gets what and who deals with things.

### Checklist for the will

- [ ] Check whether you already have a valid will.
- [ ] If you do, review it. After your wife’s death, it may need updating.
- [ ] If you don’t have one, make one. Even a simple will is better than none.
- [ ] Say that this will cancels any earlier wills or codicils.
- [ ] Name your executor and backup executor.
- [ ] Say what happens to your home, if you have one.
- [ ] Say what happens to your bank accounts, investments, pension lump sums, etc.
- [ ] Say who gets personal items: watch, tools, jewellery, photos, books, etc.
- [ ] If you have already given things away, note that clearly. For example:  
  “I gave my father’s watch to [name] on [date]. This is a completed gift.”
- [ ] Include your cat. For example:
  - Name the cat carer.
  - Leave a sum of money for the cat’s care.
  - Ask the executor to look after the cat or fund its care.
  - In some places you can set up a small “pet trust”; ask a local lawyer if that is appropriate.
- [ ] State your funeral wishes, if you want: burial, cremation, religion, music, people to speak, etc.
- [ ] Sign and witness the will correctly according to your local rules.  
  In many places this means signing in front of two witnesses who are not beneficiaries.
- [ ] Keep the original in a safe, known place.
- [ ] Tell your executor where the original is.
- [ ] Give a copy to your lawyer/solicitor or another trusted person, if appropriate.
- [ ] Do **not** put passwords, PINs, or safe-deposit box keys in the will. Wills may become public documents in some places.

A separate “letter of personal wishes” can also be helpful. It does not usually have legal force, but it can explain your feelings and practical wishes.

---

## 3. Set up power of attorney / enduring power of attorney / lasting power of attorney

This is different from a will. A will only works after death. Power of attorney helps if you are alive but unable to make decisions, for example after a serious illness, accident, stroke, or dementia.

You may want two types, depending on your country:

1. **Property and financial affairs**
2. **Health and welfare / medical care**

### Checklist

- [ ] Decide who you trust to make financial decisions if you cannot.
- [ ] Decide who you trust to make health and care decisions if you cannot.
- [ ] Appoint a primary person and a backup for each.
- [ ] Decide whether the authority starts only if you lose capacity, or whether it can start immediately.
- [ ] Write clear instructions if you want:
  - who should be told;
  - how bills should be paid;
  - whether the person can sell your home;
  - whether they can make gifts;
  - how your cat should be cared for;
  - your views on medical treatment, hospital, care home, end-of-life care.
- [ ] Complete the official forms correctly.
- [ ] Have them certified/witnessed as required.
- [ ] Register them if your country requires registration.
- [ ] Keep the original in a safe place.
- [ ] Tell your attorney where it is.
- [ ] Give a copy to your GP, if appropriate, and to your executor.

This is one of the most useful things you can do. It can prevent bank freezes, unpaid bills, and confusion if you become ill.

---

## 4. Sort out bank documents

This is where people often get stuck: too many accounts, unclear beneficiaries, forgotten direct debits.

### Make a bank list

For each bank, building society, credit union, or savings account, write down:

- [ ] Bank name
- [ ] Branch address
- [ ] Account number
- [ ] Sort code / routing number, if applicable
- [ ] Is it sole or joint?
- [ ] Who is the joint owner, if any?
- [ ] Is there a “payable on death” or nominated beneficiary?
- [ ] Approximate balance
- [ ] Regular income coming in: pension, benefits, dividends
- [ ] Regular outgoing payments: direct debits, standing orders, card payments
- [ ] Where statements are stored
- [ ] Online banking: how to access it, in a secure separate document
- [ ] Debit/credit cards: card numbers not needed, but issuer and whether to cancel
- [ ] Safe deposit box: bank, branch, key location, contents

### Practical steps

- [ ] Update beneficiaries where possible.
- [ ] Check whether any accounts are joint. If they are, the surviving joint owner may automatically inherit the account, depending on local rules.
- [ ] List direct debits and standing orders that should be stopped.
- [ ] List subscriptions that should be cancelled.
- [ ] Note whether any bank needs to be told about your will or executor.
- [ ] Keep recent statements with the rest of your papers.

Do not put full account numbers and passwords in the same place as sentimental items. Keep financial details secure but accessible to your executor.

---

## 5. List debts, loans, and mortgages

Your executor will need to know what is owed.

### Checklist

- [ ] Mortgage: lender, account number, balance, whether it’s joint.
- [ ] Car loan / hire purchase.
- [ ] Credit cards.
- [ ] Store cards.
- [ ] Personal loans.
- [ ] Overdraft.
- [ ] Any money owed to you.
- [ ] Utility accounts: electricity, gas, water, internet, phone.
- [ ] Council tax / rates, if applicable.
- [ ] Insurance premiums.
- [ ] Any family loans, formal or informal.

For each, note:

- [ ] Creditor
- [ ] Account number
- [ ] Approximate balance
- [ ] Monthly payment
- [ ] Contact details
- [ ] Whether it is joint
- [ ] What should happen after you die

If you have a mortgage, this is especially important. If the property is solely yours, your executor will need to deal with it according to your will and local law.

---

## 6. Pensions

At 58, pension planning is especially important.

### Checklist

- [ ] State pension / social security, if applicable.
- [ ] Workplace pension.
- [ ] Personal pension.
- [ ] Self-investment pension, if any.
- [ ] Annuity, if you have one.
- [ ] Any lump-sum death benefit.
- [ ] Funeral expense benefit.
- [ ] Who is named as beneficiary/nominee.
- [ ] Whether the pension provider has your up-to-date contact details.
- [ ] Where the paperwork is kept.

For each pension:

- [ ] Provider name
- [ ] Policy/account number
- [ ] Contact address/phone/email
- [ ] Nominee/beneficiary
- [ ] Last statement
- [ ] Any forms already completed
- [ ] Whether you can change the nomination now

It is worth contacting each provider and confirming your details.

---

## 7. Insurance policies

### Checklist

- [ ] Life insurance
- [ ] Critical illness insurance
- [ ] Funeral plan insurance, if any
- [ ] Home insurance
- [ ] Contents insurance
- [ ] Car insurance
- [ ] Travel insurance
- [ ] Pet insurance
- [ ] Any other policies

For each:

- [ ] Insurer
- [ ] Policy number
- [ ] Type of cover
- [ ] Sum insured
- [ ] Beneficiary, if relevant
- [ ] Renewal date
- [ ] Premium amount
- [ ] Payment method
- [ ] Where the policy is stored

For life insurance, confirm the beneficiary is who you want. If your wife was previously the beneficiary, this may need changing.

---

## 8. Property and household affairs

Whether you own or rent, make the practical side clear.

### If you own

- [ ] Title deed / ownership documents
- [ ] Mortgage documents
- [ ] Property tax / council tax / rates information
- [ ] Home insurance
- [ ] Building plans, if relevant
- [ ] Warranty/guarantee documents
- [ ] Gas/electric certificates
- [ ] Alarm/fob/key codes
- [ ] Neighbour with spare key
- [ ] Landlord/agent details, if leasehold or shared ownership

### If you rent

- [ ] Tenancy agreement
- [ ] Landlord/agent contact
- [ ] Deposit details
- [ ] Notice period
- [ ] Who should end the tenancy
- [ ] Who should return keys
- [ ] Who should deal with the landlord

### Household practicalities

- [ ] Who has keys?
- [ ] Who can collect mail?
- [ ] Who should stop utilities?
- [ ] Who should inform the bank?
- [ ] Who should inform the pension provider?
- [ ] Who should deal with the phone/internet?
- [ ] Who should arrange the funeral?
- [ ] Who should look after the cat in the short term?

You can make a simple “household instruction” sheet for your executor. It can include things like:

- where the spare key is;
- who has a key;
- which utilities are on direct debit;
- which bills are monthly;
- where the gas/electric meters are;
- who does the garden or repairs;
- whether there is a neighbour who checks in.

---

## 9. Cat care plan

Since you’ve already asked a neighbour to look after the cat, put it in writing. This avoids awkwardness later.

### Cat care document

- [ ] Cat’s name
- [ ] Age/breed
- [ ] Microchip number
- [ ] Vet name and contact details
- [ ] Emergency vet / out-of-hours vet
- [ ] Pet insurance details, if any
- [ ] Daily routine: feeding times, food type, litter, water
- [ ] Medications, if any
- [ ] Behaviour notes: shy, friendly, dislikes being carried, etc.
- [ ] Where food/litter are kept
- [ ] Where the cat carrier is
- [ ] Who has a spare key
- [ ] Who can feed the cat if the main carer is unavailable
- [ ] How much money should be available for vet costs
- [ ] Who pays the vet directly

You could write something like:

> “If I am unable to care for my cat, I ask [name] to take responsibility for [cat’s name]. I have left [amount] for food and veterinary costs. The vet is [name, address, phone]. [Backup name] can help if needed.”

This can be included with your will or kept as a separate letter to the executor.

---

## 10. Digital accounts and online access

This is easier to sort now than for someone else to do later.

### Make a digital list

- [ ] Phone number and carrier
- [ ] Email addresses
- [ ] Online banking logins
- [ ] Pension logins
- [ ] Government/benefits accounts
- [ ] Tax accounts
- [ ] Cloud storage
- [ ] Photo storage
- [ ] Social media
- [ ] Streaming services
- [ ] Online shops
- [ ] Subscriptions
- [ ] Gaming accounts
- [ ] Domain names / websites, if any
- [ ] Crypto/wallets, if any

### How to store it safely

- [ ] Use a password manager, if possible.
- [ ] Keep a separate secure list for your executor.
- [ ] Do not put it in the will.
- [ ] Tell your executor where it is.
- [ ] Decide what you want to happen:
  - close accounts;
  - cancel subscriptions;
  - memorialise social media;
  - transfer photos;
  - delete devices after a certain time.

Some services have “inactive account” or “legacy contact” settings. For example, Google, Apple, and social media platforms allow you to name a contact or make some instructions in advance.

---

## 11. Funeral and personal wishes

You don’t have to be precise, but it helps everyone if your wishes are written down.

### Checklist

- [ ] Burial or cremation preference
- [ ] Religious or spiritual wishes
- [ ] People you would like present
- [ ] Music, readings, or speakers
- [ ] Flowers or donations instead
- [ ] Donation of organs/body for medicine, if you want
- [ ] Funeral home or director, if you have one
- [ ] Pre-paid funeral plan, if any
- [ ] Who should make the arrangements
- [ ] Who should pay
- [ ] Whether you want a simple service or something more elaborate
- [ ] Any personal items you want at the service
- [ ] Any personal items you want destroyed, given away, or kept

You can leave this as a written note. It may not be legally binding, but it gives people guidance.

---

## 12. Make a master document list

This is one of the most useful things you can do. It saves your executor from hunting around.

Create a simple table:

| Document / item | Where it is kept | Who can access it | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Original will | Fireproof box at home / lawyer’s office | Executor, lawyer | Signed [date] |
| Power of attorney — financial | Drawer in study / safe | Attorney, executor | Registered [date] |
| Bank accounts list | Envelope in desk | Executor | Updated [date] |
| Pension details | File in drawer | Executor | Contact provider |
| Insurance policies | Folder in cabinet | Executor | Life insurance beneficiary updated |
| Cat care instructions | With will / given to carer | Cat carer, executor | Vet contact inside |
| Password list | Separate envelope | Executor only | Do not put in will |
| Funeral wishes | Letter in file | Executor, funeral contact | Cremation preferred |

Keep the master list in a place your executor can find. You might keep:

- one copy at home in a safe, known place;
- one copy with your lawyer;
- one copy in a separate secure location, such as with a trusted person or in a safe-deposit box.

Do not make it too hard to find. “Hidden in a secret place” can cause delay and stress.

---

## 13. Write a short “letter of instruction” for your executor

This is not a legal document, but it can be very helpful. It can include:

- who to contact first;
- where the will is;
- where the power of attorney is;
- where the bank list is;
- where the password list is;
- where the cat’s food and vet details are;
- who has keys;
- your funeral wishes;
- who should be told and in what order;
- any personal requests, such as looking after a friend, neighbour, or pet.

You might start with something like:

> “If you are reading this, I am no longer able to manage my affairs. My will is located at [place]. My power of attorney documents are at [place]. My bank details are in the envelope marked [label]. Please contact [name] about the cat. My GP is [name]. I would like [person] to be told first. My funeral wishes are in the attached note.”

Keep it short and calm. The person reading it may be stressed.

---

## 14. Deal with the things you’ve already given away

You mentioned giving your tools and your father’s watch to neighbours. That is understandable, but it can cause confusion later if it is not recorded.

Make a simple memo:

- [ ] Item
- [ ] Given to whom
- [ ] Date
- [ ] Whether it was a gift
- [ ] Any sentimental note, if you wish

For example:

> “I gave my father’s watch to [name] on [date]. I did this as a personal gift. I do not intend it to be part of my estate.”

Keep this memo with your will or letter of instructions. It does not replace the will, but it can help prevent misunderstandings.

---

## 15. Keep everything reviewed

Life changes. Even when things feel settled, it is good to review your documents:

- once a year, or
- after any major change: move, new relationship, sale of property, change in health, new debt, change in who you trust.

Each time, update:

- [ ] Will
- [ ] Power of attorney
- [ ] Bank beneficiaries
- [ ] Pension nominees
- [ ] Insurance beneficiaries
- [ ] Contact details
- [ ] Cat carer
- [ ] Funeral wishes
- [ ] Master document list

---

## A sensible order to do this

If it feels overwhelming, do it in small steps.

### This week

1. Make the list of key people.
2. List your bank accounts and debts.
3. Write down where your main documents are already kept.
4. Choose who you want to be your executor and cat carer.
5. Tell someone you trust that you are doing this.

### Next two weeks

6. Check your will. If you don’t have one, book an appointment with a local lawyer/solicitor or reputable will-writing service.
7. Check your power of attorney. If you don’t have one, ask a local professional about the correct forms.
8. Update pension and insurance beneficiaries.
9. Write the cat care plan.
10. Start the master document list.

### Within a month

11. Write the letter of instruction.
12. Secure the documents.
13. Tell your executor where everything is.
14. Review the whole thing and date it.

---

## A gentle but important note

Sorting papers can bring up a lot of grief, especially after losing your wife. It may make you more aware of being alone. If that happens, please don’t just push through it silently.

Consider:

- telling your GP that you are feeling lonely;
- asking a neighbour or friend to check in regularly;
- joining a bereavement group;
- speaking to a counsellor or therapist;
- arranging a regular social activity, even small ones: coffee, walking group, community centre, library, club, volunteer work.

Making practical arrangements is wise, but you also deserve support while you are still here.
